blocks.text: Food is a substance that can be metabolized by an organism to obtain nutrients and energy. Humans consume food for nutrition as well as for sensual pleasure. For that reason, food must be nutritious and wholesome (with proper visual appearance, flavor, and texture). Microbes, particularly various species of bacteria and fungi, can metabolize virtually any food item. The mere presence of certain microbes in food may make it unacceptable for human consumption. As microbes metabolize food items, their metabolic products and wastes accumulate in the food. As a result, the food items may lose nutritional and aesthetic qualities or even turn toxic. Food-borne illnesses are quite common in all societies. Deterioration of nutritional and aesthetic qualities of food due to undesirable biochemical changes is food spoilage. Food can be spoiled by enzymes already present in food items such as meat and vegetables, by oxidation of fat, coagulation of proteins, loss of moisture, and the presence of contaminants. Microbial growth in food is the major cause of food spoilage. However, controlled microbial spoilage can be used in preparing and preserving certain food items. Here we will discuss microbial food spoilage; proper food handling, preparation, and preservation of food; and the use of controlled microbial degradation of food items to prepare food and other useful items.
Microbes generally found in food

Microbes and some other contaminants can be an intrinsic part of certain food items. For example, worm cysts can be present in fresh meat, and algal toxins can be present in fresh seafood. Microbes and other contaminants may enter food items after harvest or preparation. For example, Staphylococcus aureus may get into prepared food from the hands of the chef. Fresh vegetables washed with contaminated water may gain pathogenic enteric viruses and bacteria. A shortlist of microbes found in common food items and the significance of such contamination is listed in Table 16.2.
Table 16.2. Harmful microbes, microbial toxins, and other harmful substances found in food substances.

Food type Common pathogenic microbes Comments Grains, oilseeds, nuts Fungi* (various species of Aspergillus, Claviceps, Phoma, Curvularia, etc.), bacteria (various species of Bacillus, Clostridium, and Erwinia). Fungi of the genera Aspergillus, Rhizopus, Mucor, Penicillium, and Monilia may grow in bread, particularly homemade and organic bread. Cooked rice supports the growth of many bacteria including the toxin- producing Bacillus cereus and some molds.

Fish and shellfish Worm eggs and larvae in the muscle of finfish; naked icosahedral viruses from the intestine may contaminate muscles during processing; Clostridia, Mycobacterium marinum in bottom-feeding fishes; vibrioids (Vibrio parahaemolyticus and V. vulnificus), and worm larvae in shellfishes.
Oysters and other filter feeders may accumulate algal toxins and enteric viruses. Only USDA-certified batches of these organisms could be consumed.

Milk and dairy products Milk- soil microbes (including pseudomonads, Clostridium perfringens, Listeria monocytogenes, Serratia marcescens), enteric bacteria (Salmonella enterica), and other bacteria (Mycobacterium bovis, and various species of Brucella, Coxiella, and Leptospira); dairy products with low sugar contents may contain soil bacteria (such as pseudomonads, Clostridium perfringens, Serratia marcescens) and Staphylococcus aureus (from hands of food handlers); the microbes may rapidly grow in the food items and some may secrete toxins in the food items.

The udders of cattle are sub- clinically infected by bacteria and fungi, pasteurized milk is safe but gets contaminated by airborne microbes during use, milk of cattle treated with growth hormones (such as bovine somatotropin) may contain slightly higher levels of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1).

Spices, condiments, and supplements Dried spices and supplements are usually sterilized (chemically or by irradiation). Raw spices (onion, garlic, zinger roots) can be colonized and spoiled by fungi and some bacteria. Honey may contain bacterial endospores (including endospores of Clostridium botulinum) Some imported spices may contain higher levels of heavy metal, herbal tea may contain soil fungi and bacterial endospores; raw honey should not be given to infants Microbial and non-microbial food spoilage Spoilage requires microbial growth in food items. Some species of microbes can spoil almost any food item, but not all food items are equally perishable. Foods are grouped as highly perishable, perishable, and non- perishable (this latter term is not quite appropriate but used in this field), based on how rapidly the food item can be spoiled by microbes. Both intrinsic (built-in) and extrinsic (externally applied) factors affect the rapidity of food spoilage (see Table 16.3). The intrinsic factors are an integral part of fresh food items. Intrinsic factors include physical barriers (such as the rind of fruits, husk of seeds and nuts, and shell of eggs, etc.), naturally occurring antimicrobial agents present in food (such as antibacterial agents in spices, antimicrobial antibodies, and enzymes present in live eggs), nutrient richness (such as vitamins), pH, and water activity. Foods of acidic pH are highly stable because most microbes either fail to grow in acidic foods or grow in them very slowly. Note that the pH of almost all natural or prepared food items is 7.0 or lower. Food items of pH above 7.5 are rare, with the exception of egg white (pH 9.0).
Water activity

Water activity (aw) is defined as the ratio of the vapor pressure of water of a food item to the vapor pressure of pure water at the same temperature. The aw of pure distilled water is 1.0, and that of tap water is ~0.99. Dissolved chemical substances reduce water activity. The higher the water activity of food, the more perishable the food item is. Thus, milk, fresh meat, and fish (aw=0.97) are more perishable than beef jerky (aw= <0.88), fruit jam (aw= 0.85), or dry fish (aw ~0.75). Most bacteria are unable to grow below an aw of 0.90, although an aw of 0.7 is required to inhibit mold growth.

Food preparation and preservation often involve (a) reduction of aw and pH, (b) addition of antimicrobial agents in food, (c) manipulation of extrinsic factors such as storage temperature, (d) removal of oxygen (to prevent oxidation and inhibit the growth of aerobes), (e) protecting from light (to inhibit light-induced chemical reactions), and (f) shielding from the environment (to prevent post-preparation contamination).
Table 16.3. Intrinsic and extrinsic factors that affect food spoilage. The factors are marked as (+) if they
inhibit spoilage, or (-) if they support rapid spoilage.

Intrinsic factors (+) Physical barriers to the environment (such as husk, rind, and shell) (+) Antimicrobial agent (such as allicin, an antibiotic found in garlic) (-) Nutrient richness (such as dissolved sugar and vitamins in raw milk) (-) High Water Activity (as in milk) (-) Neutral pH (as in milk) Extrinsic factors (+) Putting a barrier (such as canning) (+) Reducing water activity (such as drying, curing, pickling, and jellying) (+) Lowering pH (i.e., adding organic acids to food, or fermenting) (+) Prevent chemical reactions (reducing temperature, shielding from air and light) Food handling and cooking Safe handling of food involves the acquisition, storage, and preparation. USDA (see http://www.fsis.usda.gov) has excellent internet resources on food handling. Food should be handled by a healthy adult. People infected by highly infectious microbes (such as disease-causing strains of Salmonella sp., Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and hepatitis A or hepatitis B viruses) should not handle food. There are four basic rules (also called the CSCC rules, see Fig. 16.23) of food handling: • Clean (wash hands and surfaces that may come in contact with food).
• Separate (do not cross-contaminate, for example, do not allow raw meat to touch milk).
• Cook (to appropriate temperature), and • Chill (store at an appropriate temperature.

Finally, food not to be used should be discarded and safely disposed of at some point. Good food handling starts with shopping. Food should be bought from reliable vendors. While shopping, food to be refrigerated should be picked after non-perishables are already collected. The expiration date (i.e., the ‘use before’ or ‘best before’ dates) should be checked before purchasing. Perishable items should be refrigerated (or frozen if applicable) within two hours of purchase. Food should be thawed and marinated in a leak-free covered pot in a refrigerator. Spilling and aerosolization of fluid during cutting meat and fish should be avoided, and the cutting board (and any surfaces that came into contact with raw meat and fish) should be decontaminated using 6% sodium hypochlorite (Clorox®) solution. The cutting boards should be nonporous. Thawed and fully marinated food items should be cooked immediately.
Fig. 16.23. Basic (CBCC) rules of food handling. Besides the four basic steps (Clean, Separate, Cook, and
Chill), the USDA suggests two additional rules: Check and Throw Away. Image courtesy: CDC.gov.

Anthropologist Richard Wrangham (1948-) argued that humans evolved as the dominating species because they adopted cooking. Cooking reduces infection risks drastically and increases the shelf life of food significantly. Cooking is essentially heat-pasteurization, aimed at eliminating disease-causing microbes such as viruses, vegetative microbial cells, protozoan cysts, worm eggs, and larvae. Raw food items may expose consumers to numerous pathogenic microbes. A list of common food-borne illnesses is provided in Table 16.4.

Food is considered cooked if the temperature of the core of the item reaches 75°C or above. Most harmful microbes and microbial toxins are destroyed at such temperatures. Cooking at a lower temperature requires treating the food at 60°C for 30 minutes, 65°C for 10 minutes, or 70°C for 2 minutes, given that the temperature is uniformly distributed in the cooked items. Note that cooking does not inactivate prion agents, endospores of Bacillus or Clostridium, and certain heat-stable microbial toxins (such as heat-stable toxins of Staphylococcus aureus). Hot food should be served hot or kept hot (at or above 60oC) for later serving, and cold food should be served cold or kept cool (at 5-8 °C) if to be served later. Some prepared or thawed food items could be refrigerated or frozen again, but it may deteriorate the taste and texture of the food items. Perishable prepared food left open for more than two hours should be discarded.

There are local, state, and federal rules on food handling and preparation. Those rules should be consulted for events such as community feasts for senior citizens to avoid foodborne infections. Note that foodborne infections account for about 25% of all emergency hospital visits. Commercial food preparers must follow those rules and additional procedures (including Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points or HCAAP) formulated by the FDA and USDA. HCAAP rules (Table 16.5) apply to food handlers, food handling procedures, and production facilities.

blocks.text: Several microbes such as mushrooms (certain species of Basidiomycota), truffles (certain species of Ascomycota), and nori and other algae (marine algae of the phyla Rhodophyta and Phaeophyta) are harvested wild or grown and used as food. Agar and carrageenan extracted from red algae, and alginic acid extracted from brown algae, are important food ingredients. Single-cell proteins (SCP), a new food concept, were developed in the 1960s to obtain food from microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and algae (Fig. 16.24).
Fig. 16.24. Single-cell nutrients. A. The cyanobacterium Arthrospira platensis. Shown are filaments containing

a row of individual cells. Image courtesy: F Karali/Microbe Wiki. B. Fresh spirulina drinks ready for consumption. Image source: https://luxuryactivist.com/. C. Spirulina tablets sold in health food stores. Image courtesy- Wikipedia.

Since edible microbes can be grown in massive quantities at a low cost, it was thought that SCP would help solve global food shortages and malnutrition. The expectation had not been realized. Instead, SCP such as dried yeasts and Spirulina powder have become expensive nutritional supplements. Spirulina supplements are dried biomass of the cyanobacterium Arthrospira platensis (the species was previously grouped under the Genus Spirulina). The cyanobacterium is grown under controlled conditions in European countries or in freshwater ponds of tropical countries. Spirulina is consumed as a broth of live cells or dried powder suspended in water as a smoothie, or as tablets or capsules (Fig. 16.24).

Microbes have been used for producing many food items since the dawn of civilization. The primitive societies fermented perishable food items such as milk and fruits into semi-perishable and non-perishable food items such as cheese and wines without knowing the microbes involved in the process. Today, many selected or domesticated strains of microbes are used for fermentation at household or industrial scales. At certain concentrations, the fermentation end products, such as organic acids (usually lactic, acetic, and propionic acids), aldehydes (usually benzaldehyde), and alcohols (i.e., ethanol), inhibit microbial growth. Some nutrients and food calories remain in the fermented food. The microbes may also produce some other organic compounds and vitamins that add flavor and nutritional value to the fermented food items. Some common fermented foods are shown in Fig. 16.25.
Fig. 16.25. Still Life with Invisibles. Shown are some common fermented food items including fish sauce [1],

beer (alcohol-free) [2], wine vinegar [3], balsamic vinegar [4], yogurt (plain and flavored) [5a, 5b], teriyaki sauce [6], Worcestershire sauce [7], black tea [8], soy sauce [9], coffee [10], pickled olives [11], dill pickles [12], pickled jalapeno pepper [13], sauerkraut [14], cocoa in chocolate candy [15], raised bread [16], cheese (slices and shredded) [17a, 17b], turkey bologna [18]. The items were instantly assembled in the author’s kitchen, indicating the importance of microbial fermentation in the daily life of common people.
Fermented dairy products

Milk is fermented to acidophilus milk or yogurt, and milk curd is converted to cheese of various kinds. There are numerous local variations in the actual process. Here we will summarize the processes used in industrial settings in the United States.
Cultured buttermilk

Whole milk or skim milk is heated to 95 oC and then homogenized at high pressure to prevent creaming (i.e., separation of dissolved components from water). Starter culture containing Streptococcus lactis is then added to 1-2% of the milk volume and fermented for 16-20 hours till the lactic acid concentration reaches 0.9%. Buttermilk is used as a drink or in baking. A starter culture is a specific (blend of) fermenting organisms produced under controlled growth conditions, protected from undesirable microbes.
Acidophilus milk

Sweet acidophilus milk contains 2-5% (by volume) of Lactobacillus acidophilus starter culture. The mixture is used as a probiotic (live microbes used for health benefits) without fermentation, or the mixture is fermented for several days at 37 °C to produce sour acidophilus milk. Sour acidophilus milk contains 1% lactic acid. Sour cream Whole milk contains about 3.7% fat. To produce sour cream, additional milk fat is added to whole milk to a final fat concentration of 12-30%. A starter culture (1-2% by volume of Streptococcus lactis) is then added, and the mixture is fermented until the lactic acid concentration reaches 0.6%. Fermented sour cream is heated to 80oC and then homogenized under high pressure before packing.
Yogurt

A starter culture containing a 1:1 blend of Streptococcus salivarius subspecies thermophilus (ST) and Lactobacillus delbrueckii subspecies bulgaricus (SB) is added to warm milk, and the mixture is fermented at 43 °C for 4-6 hours until titratable acidity reaches 0.85-1.2%. The product is then cooled to stop fermentation. Additional milk solids (dry milk powder, concentrated skim milk, or whey), stabilizers (such as gelatin, alginate, or guar gum), sweeteners (sucrose, aspartame, etc.), and flavors (usually fruit puree) may be added before packaging.
Cheese

Milk is pasteurized, warmed, and then acidified to separate curd (mostly milk proteins) from whey (i.e., water, lipids, dissolved chemicals, and vitamins). Curding is accelerated by adding rennet (a mixture of enzymes, including chymosin, obtained from the mucosa of the fourth stomach chamber of butchered pre-weaned calves). Whey is separated from curd by straining. Curd can be used as unripened cheese, such as cottage cheese, or fermented and aged. Curd can be washed in hot water (to reduce acid), kneaded (to increase rubber-like consistency), heated (to reduce water), salted (to remove water and increase stringiness of the curd proteins), and stained (by adding food color) before fermenting.

The curd can be fermented by the microbes naturally present in the curd or after adding additional microbes (such as Propionibacterium shermanii, Penicillium roquefortii, or P. camemberti) to develop specific flavors. Aging is done in a non-sterile and moist darkroom dedicated to the purpose. Some cheese varieties are aged only for a few days, but sharp cheese varieties are aged for many months to increase total acid contents. During aging, microbial metabolites (such as organic acids, amino acids, and amines) accumulate in the cheese to provide specific flavor.
Fermented meat products

Salami, summer sausage, pepperoni, and other processed meats are usually made from chopped or ground meats, organ meats, and fat. The items are mixed with sugar, salt, spices, sodium nitrite, and a starter culture containing certain species of Lactobacillus and/or Pediococcus. The added sugar is used as a substrate for fermentation; salt prevents the growth of undesirable microbes, and sodium nitrite (NaNO2) suppresses the germination of bacterial endospores (especially the endospores of Clostridium botulinum) and enhances the reddish color of processed meat.

The ingredients are mixed thoroughly and then inserted into a cleaned intestine of slaughtered animals or a synthetic polymer casing and then fermented at an elevated temperature (~42oC) for a few days to several months. When acid concentration reaches the desired level, the meat product is smoked and/or dried. The cured meat products are consumed raw (i.e., uncooked). Sodium nitrite in processed meats may produce nitrosamines during food preparation. Nitrosamine is a carcinogen (cancer-causing agent). American Cancer Society (ACS) suggested reduced consumption of red meat and processed meat to reduce cancer risks. World Health Organization (WHO) has listed processed meats among Group 1 carcinogens (known to cause cancers in humans) based on epidemiological data.
Fermented fish

In some countries, some fish species are overabundant in certain parts of the year. The excess seasonal catch is fermented after mixing with sea salt in a large earthen vat. The vats are left under the open sky or underground for several months. The microbes already present in the fish initially rot and then ferment the contents. The liquid portion is then filtered and used as fish sauce, a common condiment for East Asian cooking. Alaskan natives ferment fish more simply, just by burying fish under two feet of soil for two weeks. The fish is then recovered and consumed as is or after freezing.
Fermented fruits and vegetables

Many fruits and vegetables, including cabbage, carrot, cucumber, turnip, eggplant, olive, lime, green mango, and garlic are fermented. Fermentation of fruits and vegetables involves pickling (i.e., curing in brine containing 8% NaCl). Lactic acid bacteria (of genera Lactobacillus, Pediococcus, Leuconostoc, etc.) abundant in raw fruits and vegetables serve as the starters. Pickling raw fruits and vegetables are common in all cultures and therefore the processes vary greatly among different societies. Sauerkraut, a European delicacy is made from cabbage. To prepare sauerkraut, shredded cabbage and salt are layered in a ratio of 100:2 (by weight) in an airtight stone jar or food-grade plastic jar with a one-way valve to release gases. Spices can be added to cabbage for flavoring, and lime or alum is added to make the pickles crunchy. After about two weeks of fermentation at room temperature, the product is canned or packaged in food-grade plastic bags. Olives contain a bitter polysaccharide, which is removed by treating with sodium hydroxide solution before pickling.
Alcoholic beverages

The main ingredient of alcoholic beverages is ethyl alcohol (i.e., ethanol). Ethanol fermentation is a major industrial activity in many countries. Homebrewing is a hobby of many individuals. Improperly home-brewed alcoholic beverages may contain methanol, a toxic chemical compound (Box 16.1). However, homebrewing has spawned a cottage industry for manufacturing alcoholic beverages in many countries. The major categories of alcoholic beverages are wine, beer, and spirits. Box 16.1: Homebrewing and methanol poisoning

Over a million US households brew alcohol at home. Homebrewing/distillation was more prevalent during 1920- 1933 when alcoholic beverages were prohibited by federal law. Homebrewing is generally safe if clean ingredients are used and proper fermentation processes are followed. A potential risk of drinking home-brewed alcohol is methanol poisoning. Ingestion of about 10 ml of methanol as a methanol-contaminated alcoholic beverage can cause permanent blindness. Ingestion of about 118 ml (about 4 ounces) of methanol is fatal. There is no known microbe used in fermentation that synthesizes methanol. However, some bacteria, yeast, and other fungi have an enzyme called pectin esterase that degrades pectin to pectate and methanol. Very low levels of methanol can be detected in various alcoholic beverages, including wines and spirits. Methanol is added to ethyl alcohol in some countries, and the product, called methylated spirit, is sold as a solvent or for other uses. Methanol can be mixed into alcoholic beverages either deliberately or by ignorance by unscrupulous traders. A small amount of methanol is present in household glass cleaners and antifreeze liquids. Methanol poisoning is quite frequent in many developing countries where ethanol drinking is prohibited by law (as in Muslim-majority countries), or ethanol is prohibitively expensive (as in Africa, South Asia, and East Asia). About a thousand people die of ethanol poisoning in India every year. Ethanol is administered as an antidote for treating methanol poisoning.
Wine

Select cultivars of red and/or white grapes of appropriate ripeness are crushed in a machine. The resulting mix of juice and solids is called must. For red wine, the must is fermented for a few days before the solids are removed. For white wine, the solids are removed before fermentation. Specific strains of yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) are added to the must for fermentation of sugar to alcohol. Wild yeasts and bacteria naturally present in the must are inhibited by adding sodium sulfite or sulfur dioxide. Fermentation is carried on at a controlled temperature and stopped when ethanol content reaches ~15%. A clear wine is then siphoned away from the vat and aged in wooden casks. The liquid is then filtered and bottled. The flavor of wine comes from chemical substances released from grape skin, grape seeds, and the wood of the casks.
Beer

Beer is made from grains (barley, wheat, rye, and rice). Grains contain only small amounts of fermentable sugars. Therefore, fermentable sugars are extracted from starches of the grain. Barley is soaked so that the seeds may germinate. Various enzymes, including amylases and proteases, are expressed during the germination process. Amylases digest starch and release fermentable sugars. The germinating grains (called malt) are then dried or roasted in a kiln and then ground to separate the kernel from the husk.

essentially identical except that in beer manufacturing, (a) hops are added, (b) sugar release from starch is regulated by boiling the mash before the fermentation process starts, and (d) alcohol is not distilled. In manufacturing spirits, sugar extraction from starch continues during fermentation, and alcohol is collected by distillation.

Water is added to the ground malt, and the resulting product, called mash, is incubated at 45-75oC for several hours. During this time, amylases (enzymes) present in the granules digest starch and release maltose, a fermentable sugar. The resulting sugary solution (called wort) is separated from the granular materials, and florets of the hop plant (Humulus lupulus) are added to it. The mixture is then boiled to inactivate the enzymes and to extract the resins of hop flowers that give beer its bitter taste.

The liquid is then cooled down and taken to a fermentation kettle. Yeast (specific strains of Saccharomyces cerevisiae) is added to initiate fermentation. Depending on the yeast strain, fermentation is performed at 15-24 oC (to produce ale beer) or at about 10 oC (to produce lager beer) for several weeks. At that time, fermentable sugars are converted to alcohol. The liquid is then cooled down to near freezing temperature to separate insoluble substances, unpleasant chemical substances, and yeast cells. Beer is then filtered and conditioned in wooden casks for several months before being packed in bottles, cans, or casks. Based on the degree of malt roasting and the filtration process, beer can be very pale yellow to deep black in coloration. Beer contains about 5% alcohol by volume, some carbohydrates, proteins, hop resins, and various metabolites of yeast. Light beers or low-point beers contain reduced (2-4%) alcohol and carbohydrate contents.
Spirits (liquors)

Spirits, grain alcohol, and ethanol in gasohol (car fuel containing 5-95% ethyl alcohol) are produced from sugar and/or starch of various plant products such as grains (including wheat, corn, and rice), fruits (such as peaches), tubers (such as potato and beet), juice and plant extracts (such as sugarcane juice or molasses and the extract of agave stem). The fermentable sugars are released from starches by the malting and mashing processes described previously for beer. For fuel-grade ethanol production, corn starch is treated with dilute sulfuric acid or fungal amylase to release fermentable sugars. The mash (or comparable liquid) is then directly fermented (without inactivating the enzymes) using high-alcohol-tolerant strains of yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae). Tequila is produced from fluid extracted from blue agave and is fermented by a bacterium (Zymomonas mobilis). After fermentation, alcohol is separated from the mash by distillation. Beverage-grade alcohol is aged in wooden casks. Other ingredients (such as juniper berry extract in gin) are mixed before bottling. Spirit or alcoholic liquors contain 35-46% alcohol by volume (alcohol content is adjusted by adding water).
Raised bread

Bread is raised by CO2 gas released during alcoholic fermentation of sugar by baker’s yeast (certain strains of S. cerevisiae). Baker’s yeast is available in supermarkets as packages of dry powder. Yeast is reconstituted by mixing a small amount of the powder with warm water and then adding it to the dough (containing flour, water, sugar, milk, butter, nuts, and other ingredients). The dough ball is placed in a pot for a few hours. During this time, yeast multiplies, ferments sugar, and produces ethanol and CO2 gas. The CO2 gas increases the size of the dough ball. Alcohol is evaporated, and yeast cells are killed during baking. A starter culture of lactic acid bacteria can be added to the dough to produce (fermented) sourdough bread.
Soy sauce

Soy sauce is made from roasted whole soybean seeds mixed with roasted cracked wheat and other grains using a variety of methods throughout East Asia. The production process varies greatly in different regions. In general, starch and proteins in the seeds are released in water and then digested to amino acids and fermentable sugars by enzymes released by the fungus Aspergillus oryzae or some other species of Aspergillus. After a few days of the treatment, salt is added to a final concentration of about 18%, and the product is aged for a year or more under the open sun or in underground silos. Salt-tolerant bacteria (such as Lactobacilli and Pediococcus sp.) and fungi grow in the vat, but no starter culture is added. The liquid portion of the aged product is separated from solids. Additional ingredients may be added before packaging. Traditionally made soy sauce may contain toxic chemicals including ethyl carbamate, a carcinogen. Industrially produced soy uses soy flour, and the fermentation process is conducted under controlled conditions.
Brewed vinegar

Vinegar (4% acetic acid by volume) is generally produced from dilute alcohol by acetic acid bacteria of the genera Acetobacter and Gluconobacter. Dilute fermented alcohol (in fermented cane juice, apple cider, must, or mashed grain) is placed in a tank, and mother of vinegar (i.e., a starter culture containing acetic acid bacteria) is inoculated into the liquid. The liquid is stirred, and the air is continuously bubbled into the liquid for oxygenation of ethanol. Under these conditions, Acetobacter sp. convert the ethyl alcohol contents of the fluid to vinegar within 1-3 days through the reaction CH3-CH2-OHà CH3COOH + H2O. Kombucha vinegar is produced from kombucha (i.e., fermented green or black tea) by a coculture of yeast and anaerobic bacteria. Spirit vinegar (also called white, distilled, or virgin vinegar) contains 5-8% acetic acid, which is produced from diluted distilled alcohol or synthetic acetic acid.
Monosodium glutamate

Monosodium glutamate (MSG) is a sodium salt of glutamic acid. Glutamate is present in almost all foods in low concentration (for example, Roquefort cheese may contain 1.0% w/w free glutamate). MSG is used as a flavor enhancer, particularly for industrially manufactured foods. MSG is industrially produced by specific strains of the bacterium Micrococcus glutamicus grown in a nutrient broth. The bacterium releases excess MSG in the culture medium. Crystalline MSG is separated from the culture broth. MSG or other forms of glutamates are generally safe in low concentrations. However, glutamate is a neurotransmitter; excess intake of glutamate has been associated with excitability, neck pain, nausea, and some other symptoms in humans and blindness in test animals.
Brewed hot sauce

Most of the chili sauces sold in the market are a mixture of chili paste, vinegar, and spices. However, chili pepper paste can be fermented by anaerobic bacteria naturally present on fresh chili peppers to produce hot sauces. Spices are added to the fermented chili paste before packaging.
Other fermented products

Many other products are produced through fermentation. Retting of jute plants to separate jute fibers, production of black tea from tea leaves, separating cocoa beans from cocoa pods, and separating coffee beans from coffee cherries involve microbial fermentation. A few of the additional products are described here.

5. Microbiology of food Preservation

The main objectives of food preservation are (a) preventing spoilage, (b) preventing the accumulation of microbial toxins, (c) retaining nutritional and aesthetic properties, and (d) increasing the shelf life of food. Some of the principles applied in food preservation are described in Chapter 7. Only specific food preservation procedures are briefly described here.
Pasteurization

Pasteurization involves treatments that kill vegetative cells of pathogenic microbes. Cooking food at modest temperatures is essentially pasteurization. Milk, some dairy products, and meat products are heat-pasteurized; fruit juices are cold pasteurized using high pressure (see Chapter 5). The process increases the shelf life of highly perishable food items. Bacterial endospores and heat-resistant bacteria (such as Bacillus stearothermophilus) may remain viable in pasteurized milk and juice and ultimately spoil them by the time the shelf life approaches. Canning: Vacuum packing and nitrogen packing Canning is packing food items in airtight glass, metallic, or plastic containers under reduced pressure. Foods of acidic pH are cooked, but food items of neutral pH are autoclaved (to inactivate Clostridium botulinum endospores) before canning. Low oxygen tension in the cans reduces the rate of spoilage by oxidation. Home- canning of non-acidic food items is discouraged because Clostridium botulinum spores may germinate and release botulinum toxin in the can. Fortunately, botulinum toxin can be deactivated by boiling or cooking the suspected canned food for 5 minutes at 70 oC.

Potato chips, nuts, salad mixes, fruits, lunch meats, and some frozen foods are packed in non-porous airtight bags or containers. To prevent oxidation and spoilage of packed items, air is removed from the package and replaced by nitrogen gas. Since nitrogen is an inert gas, nitrogen-packed foods remain fresh for a longer period. Refrigeration and freezing Low heat reduces microbial growth. However, psychrotrophs such as Listeria monocytogenes continue to grow in refrigerators. Worm eggs and larvae naturally found in the meat of domesticated animals are generally killed at freezing conditions if stored at -15 oC for 20 days or -21 oC or below for 1-7 days. Eggs and larvae of worms in meats of game animals and wild-caught freshwater fishes may or may not be killed at these temperatures. Brief exposure of meat to liquid nitrogen may kill eggs and larvae of some worms.

Foods frozen for prolonged periods may suffer from freezer burn due to dehydration and oxidative damage to the food. Food containing unsaturated fatty acids (such as fatty fishes) becomes rancid due to oxidation of unsaturated fats. Self-defrosting freezers should not be used for storing frozen food because repeated heat-thaw cycles the machines conduct damage food texture due to crystallization of water inside the food and thawing of the ice crystals.

Drying, pickling, and preserving in thick syrup These processes reduce water content (i.e., water activity) and increase osmotic pressure. Vegetative bacterial cells fail to grow if water activity (aw) is 0.9 or lower, and most fungi fail to grow at aw of 0.7 or lower. Food irradiation Gamma rays passing through food items would kill/inactivate microbes by destroying DNA and RNA. However, intense gamma rays may alter the taste, flavor, and consistency of food. FDA has approved the isotope 60Co27 for irradiation of various food items (Table 16.7) because the cobalt isotope has a half-life of about 5 years, it generates strong gamma radiation, the isotope is easy to manufacture and dispose of, but the isotope is not fissile (the isotope does not break/ create other radioactive nuclides).

Many developed countries routinely irradiate fruits, grains, spices, and seasonings to eliminate worms, insects and their eggs and larvae, and other microorganisms. The US Military uses irradiated meat for military rations. Irradiated fruits and meats (Fig. 16.27) are gradually being accepted by US consumers.
Acidification of food
Most pathogenic microbes fail to grow at a pH below 4.5. Adding vinegar (5% acetic acid), lactic acid, and other organic acids to food reduces pH and prevents microbial spoilage.

Adding antimicrobial agents to food

Organic acids (such as benzoic acid), bacterial colicins, and antibiotics (such as nisin and natamycin) prevent the growth of certain species of bacteria. Sodium nitrite prevents germination of bacterial endospores, especially endospores of Clostridium botulinum. Spices, including ginger, garlic, onion, and turmeric, contain some antimicrobial agents that suppress microbial growth and thus increase the shelf-life of prepared food. Extraction of useful biochemicals from microbes Various useful products, including polysaccharides, proteins, and enzymes, are extracted from bacterial and fungal cells. These products have medical, biological, and industrial applications. The yield of these products can be enhanced through genetic selection or genetic manipulation of the microbes (see Chapter 6). Recombinant bacteria and fungi are significant sources of valuable recombinant polypeptides, including hormones such as insulin, human growth hormone, and follicle-stimulating hormones used in animal breeding; antigens like those found in hepatitis B vaccines; cytokines such as recombinant erythropoietin used to treat anemia; and antibodies, including Humira® for rheumatoid arthritis. In the industrial manufacturing of recombinant proteins, recombinant microorganisms are cultivated in large tanks under controlled growth conditions. The cells are harvested and then lysed to release their contents. The proteins are separated from the extract using chromatographic methods. Recently, yeast cells have been engineered to produce a complete range of human antibodies.
